omnibus_nss.category: Seat booking · team project at CTU FEL
omnibus_nss.headline: Two passengers, one seat, no double booking
omnibus_nss.pitch: A bus booking system with a live seat map. When two people grab the same seat at the same moment, only one of them gets it.
omnibus_nss.credit: Team semester project at CTU FEL by Mykhailo Plokhin and Ivan Shestachenko. A demo, not a real carrier.

overbooking.label: Double bookings
overbooking.note: The design target: the database refuses the second writer instead of a cleanup job fixing it later.

lock.label: Seat lock
lock.note: A pessimistic row lock on the seat query (BookedSegmentRepository).

deploy.label: Runs on
deploy.note: Containers on a k3s cluster — the address linked from this page.

problem.lede: Booking systems break exactly when two people want the same thing at the same time — which is also when the business earns money.
points: If the app reads a seat and then writes it, two requests can both see it free and both book it.
Overbooking is often repaired afterwards with a nightly job and an apology, instead of being impossible in the first place.
Passengers and dispatchers need different rights, not the same endpoint behind a different screen.

design.lede: One service owns reservations and nothing else writes a seat. A contested seat goes through one short transaction that holds a row lock.

solutions.why: The second request waits instead of overwriting, and the wait is short because the hold is the only work in the transaction. Optimistic retries were the alternative; on a full route they turn into a storm of retries.
The timetable, the seat map and the dispatcher only read. With a single writer, "one seat, one passenger" is a rule the system can actually check.
Spring Security resolves the role before the handler runs, so a dispatcher action cannot be reached from a passenger URL.

results.lede: Omnibus is a university project with a live demo, not a commercial service. Measured figures are checked in the code; a target is what it is designed for.

race.a: Passenger A books seat 12. The database locks that row.
race.b: Passenger B asks for seat 12 at the same moment and waits for the lock.
race.c: A's booking commits. B is told the seat is taken, not double-booked.

boowie.headline: Books and audiobooks in one app, even offline
boowie.pitch: Reads EPUB, FB2 and PDF and plays MP3 and M4B audiobooks. Books stay on the phone and open without internet; the built-in store has 20 free classics.
boowie.credit: Personal project by Mykhailo Plokhin. Installs from the browser on Android and iPhone.

formats.label: Formats
formats.note: EPUB, FB2, PDF, MP3 and M4B, plus ZIP archives of them.

store.label: Free books
store.note: Public-domain titles in the built-in store; the audiobooks are narrated with RHVoice.

offline.label: Works
offline.note: A service worker caches the app, and books are stored on the device.

problem.lede: Most readers handle either text or audio, want an account, or break on real-life files: odd encodings, zipped folders, MP3s without chapters.
points: Russian FB2 files come in windows-1251 or koi8-r, often mislabelled.
An audiobook is usually a folder of files, or a ZIP made by the iPhone Files app.
Reading and listening to the same book means two positions to keep in step.

design.lede: Everything runs in the browser. Files go through the same parsers whether they come from the phone or the store; records go to IndexedDB, large files to the browser's private file system.

solutions.choice: Parse books in the browser, no server
solutions.why: Books never leave the device, and there is no backend to run or pay for.
An audiobook folder zipped on an iPhone can be gigabytes. Reading entries as a stream keeps them out of memory, including ZIP64 archives and Russian file names.

solutions.choice: Large files in the private file system
solutions.why: The Origin Private File System holds big files without the limits of older storage; older iOS Safari falls back to IndexedDB.

solutions.choice: One position for text and audio
solutions.why: When a book has an audio edition, switching maps the place by chapter and by how far into it you were.

results.lede: Boowie is live: open it on a phone and add it to the home screen. Every figure here is checked in the code or on the live app.

wovie_next.headline: Find a film, keep a watchlist
wovie_next.pitch: A film catalogue with genres, TMDB ratings, favourites and watchlists, built to stay fast on top of a large third-party catalogue.
wovie_next.credit: Personal project by Mykhailo Plokhin. Work in progress.

route.label: Page change
route.note: The target for moving between pages — not measured yet.

revalidate.label: Catalogue refresh
revalidate.note: Catalogue pages are rendered once and refreshed every hour.

problem.lede: A film catalogue is mostly someone else's data. The work is keeping it fast and reliable when that source is slow or changes.
points: Fetching TMDB on every visit makes TMDB's bad day your bad day.
Rendering everything in the browser makes a slow phone wait for the first poster.
Watchlists belong to one person, so they cannot be cached like the catalogue.

design.lede: Catalogue pages render on the server and are cached for an hour. Only personal data — favourites and watchlists — reads the database.

solutions.choice: Cache catalogue pages for an hour
solutions.why: The catalogue is the same for everyone, so it is rendered once an hour instead of on every visit. If TMDB is down, visitors see slightly older data instead of an error.

solutions.choice: Film pages rendered on the server
solutions.why: Film pages, Top Rated and New Releases arrive as HTML, so a slow phone is not left waiting for JavaScript. The main browse page is still rendered in the browser — next on the list.

solutions.choice: The database only for personal data
solutions.why: Favourites and watchlists need real per-person reads; everything else stays out of the database.

results.lede: Wovie is a work in progress with a public demo, and its source is open.
